sectionToMerge.h2: Frequently Asked Questions About SBRT and SABR: High-Dose, Few-Fraction Radiation
sectionToMerge.intro: SBRT and SABR deliver high, precisely targeted radiation doses in just a few sessions to treat selected tumors. These FAQs explain how the treatment works, who may be suitable, and what international patients should know.

items.a: SBRT, or stereotactic body radiation therapy, delivers very high, precisely targeted radiation doses to a tumor in just a few sessions. It uses advanced imaging and treatment planning to focus radiation on the tumor while limiting exposure to nearby healthy tissue. SBRT is used for certain small, well-defined tumors in the lung, liver, spine, and other sites, and suitability depends on tumor size, location, and specialist review.

items.q: What does SABR mean and how is it different from SBRT?
items.a: SABR, or stereotactic ablative radiotherapy, is essentially another name for SBRT, and the two terms are often used interchangeably. Both describe high-dose, few-fraction radiation aimed precisely at a tumor to achieve a strong local effect. The word "ablative" highlights the intent to destroy the targeted tumor tissue. Any differences are usually regional or historical rather than clinical, and your radiation oncology team can explain the terminology they use.

SBRT works by focusing many precisely aimed radiation beams onto a tumor from different angles, concentrating a high dose where they meet. Detailed CT, MRI, or PET imaging maps the tumor, and image guidance during treatment helps account for movement, including breathing. This precision allows a strong dose to the tumor while sparing surrounding tissue. The exact technique and dose depend on tumor type, size, and location, decided by the treating team.

items.q: Which cancers can be treated with SBRT?
items.a: SBRT may be considered for selected early-stage or limited tumors in the lung, liver, spine, prostate, pancreas, adrenal glands, and some sites of oligometastatic disease. It is generally suited to small, well-defined tumors that can be targeted accurately. It is not appropriate for every cancer or every patient. Whether SBRT is suitable depends on cancer type, stage, tumor location, previous treatment, overall health, and review by a qualified radiation oncology team.

Eligibility for SBRT depends on tumor size, location, cancer type, stage, previous treatments, and overall health. It may be suitable for selected patients with small, well-defined tumors, or for those who cannot undergo surgery. Tumors near critical organs or that are large or poorly defined may not be suitable. Final decisions are made by the treating radiation oncology team after reviewing imaging, pathology, and the patient's medical condition.

items.q: How many treatment sessions does SBRT involve?
items.a: SBRT is typically delivered in a small number of sessions, often between one and five, compared with the many sessions used in conventional radiation. Each session is called a fraction, and the exact number depends on tumor type, size, location, and the planned dose. Some tumors are treated in a single session, while others need several over one to two weeks. The treating team decides the schedule after planning your treatment.

items.q: How long does each SBRT session take?
items.a: Each SBRT session usually takes about 30 minutes to an hour, though the actual radiation delivery is often shorter. Extra time is needed for careful positioning, imaging, and confirming the tumor's location before treatment begins. Sessions are painless, and you lie still while the machine delivers the beams. The total time can vary by center, equipment, and tumor site, and your radiation therapy team will explain what to expect.

items.q: What are the side effects of SBRT?
items.a: Side effects of SBRT depend on the treated area but often include fatigue and mild skin or local reactions near the site. Lung treatment may cause cough or breathlessness, while liver or abdominal treatment may cause nausea. Most side effects are manageable, though some develop weeks later. Serious effects are less common but possible. Your radiation oncology team should discuss the specific risks for your tumor site and how they can be managed.

The cost of SBRT varies widely by country, hospital, technology used, and number of sessions, so a single fixed price cannot be quoted reliably. Final cost also depends on diagnosis, tumor site, imaging, planning, any complications, and length of stay. Some centers charge per course rather than per session. For an accurate estimate, request a personalized quote from the treating hospital based on your reports and planned treatment protocol.

SBRT is available at several advanced cancer centers in India equipped with modern linear accelerators and stereotactic systems. Major hospitals in cities such as Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, and Bengaluru offer this treatment for selected tumors. Availability, technology, and expertise vary between centers, so it is important to choose a facility experienced in stereotactic radiation. Suitability and the specific plan are determined by the treating radiation oncology team after reviewing your case.

SBRT is offered in many countries with advanced radiation oncology facilities, including India, the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, Turkey, Singapore, South Korea, and China, among others. Access depends on the availability of stereotactic-capable equipment and trained specialists at a given center. Treatment quality can vary, so patients often compare technology, experience, and cost. Where treatment is appropriate should always be confirmed with a qualified oncology team after medical review.

items.q: What machines are used to deliver SBRT?
items.a: SBRT is delivered using advanced radiation systems such as modern linear accelerators with image guidance, CyberKnife, and specialized platforms like TrueBeam or Edge. These machines combine precise beam shaping, imaging, and, in some cases, motion tracking to target tumors accurately. The choice of system depends on tumor site, movement, and the center's equipment. Your radiation oncology team can explain which technology they use and why it suits your particular tumor.

items.q: How does SBRT compare to conventional radiation therapy?
items.a: SBRT differs from conventional radiation by delivering much higher doses per session over far fewer visits, using greater precision. Conventional radiation typically uses many smaller daily treatments across several weeks. SBRT's accuracy allows a strong tumor dose while sparing nearby tissue, which can be convenient for suitable patients. However, it is not appropriate for all tumors. The best approach depends on cancer type, location, and review by the treating oncology team.

items.q: Can SBRT be used for oligometastatic cancer?
items.a: SBRT may be considered for oligometastatic cancer, where only a limited number of metastatic tumors are present. In selected patients, targeting these few sites with high-dose radiation aims to control disease and, in some cases, delay progression. This approach is used alongside other treatments and depends on the number, size, and location of metastases. Whether it is appropriate should be decided by a multidisciplinary oncology team after full assessment.

items.q: Are there clinical trials for SBRT?
items.a: Yes, clinical trials continue to study SBRT for various cancers, combinations with immunotherapy or drugs, and its role in oligometastatic disease. Participation does not guarantee enrollment or benefit, as trials have strict inclusion and exclusion criteria. Eligibility is decided after medical record review and investigator assessment. Patients interested in trials should discuss options with their oncology team and review trusted trial registries to find studies relevant to their situation.

items.q: What reports are needed to plan SBRT?
items.a: Planning SBRT usually requires recent diagnostic imaging such as CT, MRI, or PET scans, along with pathology or biopsy reports confirming the diagnosis. Details of previous treatments, current medications, and overall health assessments are also important. Clear, up-to-date reports help the radiation oncology team judge suitability and design an accurate plan. Requirements can vary by center and tumor site, so confirm the exact documents needed with the treating hospital.

items.q: How can international patients access SBRT?
items.a: International patients can access SBRT by sharing medical reports with a suitable center for review, then arranging travel if the team confirms treatment is appropriate. Access depends on hospital acceptance, medical review, visa approval, travel fitness, and the patient's condition, none of which can be guaranteed. Planning should include a second opinion, estimated cost, treatment timeline, and follow-up care. Final decisions rest with the treating oncology team after full assessment.

items.q: How does CancerFax help patients with SBRT and SABR?
items.a: CancerFax helps patients organize medical reports, identify relevant specialists or treatment centers, estimate possible costs, and coordinate second opinions, appointments, travel, visa, and follow-up support. Treatment decisions are always made by the qualified oncology team after reviewing the patient's diagnosis, stage, tumor location, previous treatment, and overall health. This support is intended to guide and simplify the process, not to replace the assessment and care provided by doctors and hospitals.
